body.p: We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments. We acknowledge the limitations of our study, as well as the specific features that distinguish it from other reproducibility projects.

disp-quote.p: Main concerns:

(1) Although a number sensitivity analyses have now been conducted in order to address reviewer comments, these have been relegated to the supplementary material. Their existence is acknowledged in the multivariable model section, but the actual results of the main analysis are not mentioned at all in the main text and not taken into account in the discussion. Thus, the casual reader is not made aware of how particular results are dependent on analysis choices.

Although the main finding of the correlation between replicability and university ranking holds over nearly all the analyses conducted, others are not as consistent. The association of irreplicability with trophy journals, for instance, is not statistically significant in the multivariate model (suggesting that it may have been partially due to confounding of journal tier with institutional ranking). It becomes even weaker when unchallenged claims are removed from the analysis (see point 2 below). Similarly, the association of irreplicability with "exploratory" career style is already weak in the univariate analysis and becomes even more marginal in the multivariable model. The effect of the lead author having been a first author in the field, on the other hand, is stronger than that of journal impact factor or that of the continuity/exploratory style (even though it fails to reach formal significance), but seems to receive less attention in the discussion.

These differences in strength of evidence could be made more clear both in the abstract and in the discussion, which seem to prioritize some trends over others when discussing results. Once more, presenting a brief description of how results are affected by the sensitivity analyses in the results would be important to make these nuances clearer to the reader.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have now summarized the sensitivity analyses in the main text, and revised the abstract, Results and Discussion so that differences in strength of evidence between predictors are explicit.
In Results, we added:

“Notably, as whether a claim is followed up is not random, we refitted the model excluding unchallenged claims (Supplementary S4). This model answers a different question: the probability of failure once a claim has been tested, which removes the detection component but conditions on a selection that depends on the same predictors. The Top-50 universities association was nearly unchanged (OR 3.34, 94% HDI 1.28–9.01), whereas the trophy-journal association was smaller (OR 1.47 vs 1.75). The association with Top-50 universities remains robust in all our analyses except when using only the classifications available before our experimental validation (Supplementary S7), although with only 28 challenged claims this analysis has little power.”
And

“Taken together, the model confirms our descriptive data analysis, namely that it is the prestige of institution, and possibly publication in trophy journals, rather than the personal characteristics of the scientists that best predicts which claims will later prove to be irreplicable.” In the Abstract, we replaced

“We also found that high-impact journals and top-ranked institutions are more likely to publish challenged claims” with “We also found that claims from top-ranked institutions were more likely to be challenged and that claims published in trophy journals showed a similar but weaker trend”.
In the Discussion we changed:

“Our retrospective analysis identifies several criteria that correlate with irreplicability, although with different strengths of evidence. […] Of the factors included in the multivariable model, only top-50 institutional ranking was credibly associated with irreplicability across most sensitivity analyses. The trophy-journal and research-style associations were weaker and should be considered tentative. In contrast, having published as first author in another laboratory within the field might be associated with higher replicability (OR 0.39, 94% HDI 0.12–1.18), a trend stronger than those for journal tier or research style.”
We also removed the statement that publication in high-impact (non-trophy) journals correlates with higher replicability.

disp-quote.p: (2) I still do not understand the authors' choice of including unchallenged claims along with verified ones in the multivariate model used to investigate predictors of replicability. In particular, the justification given for this choice in the supplementary material (i.e. the fact that a finding remaining unchallenged is not a random event and might be influenced by variables such as journal tier and institutional ranking) actually seems like an additional reason for not including unchallenged claims along with verified ones: if findings from low-tier journals or less prestigious institutions are more likely to remain unchallenged, this could lead to a spurious claim of "less irreplicability" in these journals and institutions, which could be purely due to receiving less attention. Predictably, both associations are reduced when unchallenged claims are removed (although the reduction is much more marked in the journal case) in the sensitivity analysis (whose results, again, are only mentioned in the supplementary material).

Moreover, multiple other statements by the authors themselves concerning unchallenged claims seem to contradict their own decision. In multiple points in the text, they reiterate that remaining unchallenged is associated with less replicability (as suggested by the fact that replicability rates were lower in prospective replications than in the literature, even for non-suspicious claims). The decision to include unchallenged claims along with verified ones thus seems unjustified - if anything, I'd have expected the opposite approach after reading the discussion. That said, I'd argue that the best decision would be to exclude them from the analysis, as done in Figure S4, and presenting this model as the main one.

body.p: We agree with the reviewer that remaining unchallenged is not a random event. Differences in attention and follow-up may influence whether a claim is classified as challenged, and these processes may themselves be associated with journal tier or institutional ranking. Thus, a lower proportion of challenged claims cannot be interpreted directly as greater underlying replicability. Our primary model estimates the probability that a claim is classified as challenged given the evidence available through our assessment. This outcome includes the process through which problems are detected. Including unchallenged claims in the reference category does not imply that we regard them as verified. Excluding them addresses a different question: the probability of being classified as challenged among claims that were followed up. We retain this analysis as an important complementary comparison. However, because follow-up is not random, the findings in this subset cannot necessarily be generalized to all claims. Our experimental tests of 45 previously unchallenged claims provide additional evidence beyond the published literature, but their selection was also nonrandom and therefore does not eliminate this limitation. We have kept the model including all claims as our primary analysis because it describes which claims have been classified as challenged across the full corpus. We now report the model excluding unchallenged claims alongside it in the Results, and clarify that neither analysis directly estimates underlying replicability across all claims:

A major strength of this study is the focus on a subfield, the detailing of identifying the main, major, and minor claims - which is a very challenging manual task - and then cataloging not only their assessment of if these claims were followed up in the literature, but also what characteristics might be contributing to reproducibility, which also included more manual effort to supplement the data that they were able to extract from the published papers. While this provides a rich dataset for analysis, there is a major weakness with this approach, which is not unique to this study.

The main weakness is relying heavily on the published literature as the source of whether a claim was determined to be verified or not. Nonetheless it is understandable why the authors took this approach - it is the only way to get at a breadth of the literature. However, there are many documented issues with this stemming from every field of research - such as publication bias, selective reporting, all the way to fraud. Importantly, this limitation is highlighted throughout the paper. At the same time, it is not reasonable to expect this study to have conducted independent experimental replications for all 400 papers identified as this would have been a laborious and costly effort. To overcome this weakness, the authors leveraged their own expertise, and crowdsourcing within the Drosophila immunity community, to assess the validity of the claims. While this helps mitigate some of this weakness, it does introduce new challenges in interpretation, which is acknowledged in the limitations section of the discussion. Overall, this situates this study more as an expert assessment of the replicability of the published literature opposed to an assessment of independent experimental replications.

body.p: We fully agree with the reviewer that this replicability project is an expert assessment of the replicability of the published literature opposed to an assessment of independent experimental replications. We have now used this term in our abstract and discussion.

In this abstract we mentioned: “This project represents an expert assessment of the replicability 14 years later, of the replicability of nearly all publications across an entire scientific community in experimental life sciences.”

As already clearly stated in the discussion, we do not take the literature at face value and use our knowledge fruit of discussion at meeting or past experience in the lab. Notably, some of the claims we identify as challenged originate from highly cited articles, which could lead a naïve reader to assume their validity.

We also mentioned that since the launch of the website, we have received three comments from the community—one addressing a major claim and two addressing more minor points—which have led us to refine our conclusions. The limited feedback we received suggest a broad agreement of the community with our assessment. It illustrates the value of maintaining an open, community-driven resource. The public and evolving nature of the project is, in our view, a key strength.
We added in the discussion:
“The ReproSci project presents an in-depth expert analysis of reproducibility in an experimental science field with a retrospective period of 14 years.”

“Since the website was launched more than two years ago, we have received only three community comments—one on a major claim and two on minor points— prompting us to refine our conclusions. Although this could reflect limited community engagement, it may equally suggest that our assessments are largely accepted.”

disp-quote.p: The authors should be applauded for the monumental effort they put into this project, which does a wonderful job of having experts within a subfield engage their community to understand the connectiveness of the literature and attempt to understand how reliable specific results are and what factors might contribute to them. This project provides a nice blueprint for others to build from as well as leverage the data generated from this subfield and thus should have an impact in the broader discussion on reproducibility and reliability of research evidence.

body.p: We are grateful to the reviewer for this comment and for recognizing the scale of the work — this was indeed a major endeavor.

disp-quote.p: (1) Although the fact that the data mostly come from a retrospective analysis of the literature is now mentioned in the abstract and discussion, it is still strangely absent from the limitations section. Other limitations, such as the possibility of confounding between the various predictors of irreplicability (journal tier, institutional ranking) and the existence of replications in the literature, could also be addressed in this section.

body.p: This is a good point and we added in the limitation section at the end of the discussion the following sentence: ‘Third, our conclusions rest largely on retrospective data from the literature. A further limitation is the possible confounding among the predictors of irreplicability themselves (journal tier, institutional ranking, etc.)’.

disp-quote.p: (2) The paper has now been revised in order to adhere to the use of "replication/replicability" rather than "reproduction/reproducibility" for experimental replications, which is fine. But given the inconsistency in how such terms are defined in the literature, it would be useful if the authors can state upfront their definition of a "replication" in the introduction.

body.p: To address this point, we have moved from the result section to the introduction the following sentence: ‘This expert assessment project focuses on assessing the strength of the claims themselves (i.e. “indirect reproducibility” or “conceptual replicability”) rather than testing whether the original methods produce repeatable results (“direct reproducibility”). Thus, our conclusions do not directly challenge the initial results leading to a claim, but rather the general applicability (i.e. generalizability) of the claim itself (Goodman et al., 2016; Meng, 2020).’

disp-quote.p: I also note that in some points of the paper, the terminology is still confusing. In the end of the "Methodology and Claim assessment", for example, they alternate between "reproducibility" and "replicability" as synonyms, apparently with no particular reason. And in the discussion, "we observed a decreased proportion of unchallenged claims in articles published in high-impact and trophy journals indicating that claims published in these journals are more replicable" seems to convey the wrong impression (I'm assuming the authors mean "are more likely to be subject to a replication attempt", but this is clearly not the same as being "replicable".

body.p: We have been careful to avoid the term reproducible/reproducibility when discussing our study

We agree that the sentence on high-impact journals was not clear. We changed it for “Our study shows that claims published in high-impact and trophy journals are less likely to remain unchallenged, which may reflect a greater number of replication attempts on these claims.”

disp-quote.p: (3) In their responses to reviewers, the authors mention some numbers about how frequently claims were contested by the community which seem to be relevant for interpreting their findings, but this is not mentioned anywhere in the article itself. Shouldn't this be added somewhere.

body.p: Good point, we have added in the discussion: “Since the website was launched more than two years ago, we have received only three community comments—one on a major claim and two on minor points—prompting us to refine our conclusions. Although this could reflect limited community engagement, it may equally suggest that our assessments are largely accepted.”

disp-quote.p: (4) I still think that the fact that the field is more prone to publicly challenging findings from newcomers is a possibility to explain the effect of having been a first author in a Drosophila paper on replicability and that this should be mentioned as a possibility (and I don't think that the fact that there is no difference between junior and senior PIs, as cited in the authors in their responses to reviewers, fully alleviates this concern).

body.p: We have slightly modified our text in the discussion to underline this point: “In contrast, we observed a trend toward higher replicability when PIs had been first authors in the laboratories where they received their training in Drosophila immunity. This finding is consistent with the value of traditional scientific training pathways, in which early-career researchers develop their expertise within established research environments before gaining independence. Conversely, it suggests that researchers entering a field without such prior experience may face greater challenges in producing replicable findings.”

disp-quote.p: (5) Some issues that were mentioned as having been addressed in the response letter were actually unchanged in the main manuscript. For instance:

(a) The distinction between continuity and exploratory PIs has not been explained further (i.e. it would still be useful to know what it means to "be working in Drosophila immunity" - how long does an author have remain without publishing in the topic for their style to be considered "exploratory"?).

body.p: We believe that the text in the methods is clear: ‘Continuity and exploratory PIs were manually classified according to their PubMed publication list. Continuity PIs are PIs that have continued to work in the Drosophila immunity field until now or to the end of their scientific career (deceased, retired, left academia). Exploratory PIs are PIs that have done a transient incursion in the Drosophila immunity field, moving to other topics of research.’

This is clearly an expert assessment of colleagues that have left the field. Of note, nearly all the pioneer PIs in the field of Drosophila immunity were ‘continuity PI’. Among the newcomers that join the field when ‘popular’, some stay in the field while other left it.

disp-quote.p: (b) The very long paragraph in pages 22 and 23 is still very long and was not broken down.

body.p: We could not identify this paragraph
Sorry for missing this comment. We have cut the long paragraph in pages 22-23 in two. We also took this opportunity to split three long sentences in shorter ones.

disp-quote.p: (6) In the multivariable model description, the mention to the multivariable model using "unchallenged as outcome" (i.e. the one shown in Figure S3) occurs in the middle of the description of the main model (i.e. using replicability as the outcome) in a very confusing way. To an inattentive reader, this may suggest that the odds ratio presented refers to the main model (as the effect of the continuity/exploratory distinction in the main model is not mentioned). It would be clearer to present the results for the main model first (including the odds ratio for this variable) and then adding a description of the model with the alternative outcome (which is also in line with the comment on making the results for the supplementary analysis more explicit in the text).

body.p: We agree with the reviewer. We have moved the additional model and sensitivity test to the end of the Results section, so it no longer appears in the middle.

disp-quote.p: (7) In the model with "unchallenged" as the outcome (Figure S3), there seems to be a very strong effect of publication date based on the figure, but this is discussed nowhere in the text (which only considers the much weaker effect of career style.

body.p: This was actually discussed in the result section when we mentioned ‘Interestingly, we observed a peak in verified claims between 1992 and 2001, accompanied by a lower percentage of unchallenged claims (Figure 3). This period coincided with the early expansion of the field when many researchers worked on similar research questions with a relatively narrow conceptual framework of innate immunity. The subsequent increase in unchallenged claims may reflect the rapid conceptual expansion of the field, which likely outpaced the growth in the number of researchers, reducing opportunities for overlapping or validating research efforts.’

We decided to highlight this point in the discussion by adding the following text: “We observed a strong effect of publication date on the proportion of unchallenged claims (Figure S3). We hypothesize the low proportion of unchallenged claims around 1992-2001 coincided with the early expansion of the field when many researchers worked on similar research questions. The subsequent increase in unchallenged claims could result from the rapid expansion of the field, limiting the possibility of overlapping research that would validate them.”

disp-quote.p: (8) There are some points in which minor edits can be made to the text:
(a) In the multivariate analysis section, there is a mention to "lead author with an exploratory lifestyle", but I'd assume the authors mean career style here.

body.p: Good point! corrected.

disp-quote.p: (b) In the discussion, "Notably, we find that even highly cited articles-often perceived as particularly robust-contain claims that have later been challenged. However, the categories we are using in this project do not capture all issues related to replicability, but the conceptual validation of the claims.". I could not understand the logical flow here: why the "however", if the second sentence seems to bear no relation to the first one?

body.p: Good point, we have readjusted the text: “Finally, it should be underlined that the categories we are using in this project do not capture all issues related to replicability, but the conceptual validation of the claims.”

disp-quote.p: (c) For the categorical comparison tables in section 8 of the Supplementary Material, please fix formatting so that words are not broken down.

body.p: This has been done

disp-quote.p: (d) The description of the Gini coefficient analysis in the Supplementary Material mentions that "full results are reported in Supplementary", which is nonsensical and seems to have been pasted from the main text.

body.p: Good point. Changed made.

disp-quote.p: The authors have done a wonderful job of checking and updating their results and refining their manuscript. They have addressed my prior comments well and I hope the authors found them helpful in their revision process.

A key aspect though that I want to note, which is reflected in my revised public review, is the nuance of the comment on the weakness of this study (i.e., taking the published literature at face value). My comment on this was not about treating aspects of the literature, like citations, as a proxy for replicability. Rather, it was about leveraging the literature and not challenging it directly through independent empirical replications (although this was done for a subset of unchallenged claims (45 major and 11 minor)). I think another way of framing this is that for this study the assessment of replicability from the literature was done by expert assessment of the literature (and tacit knowledge) opposed to independent experimental replications. This is not to suggest one is 'better' than the other, more that they have different interpretations and limitations. Personally, I think both are valuable and have huge value when done simultaneously.

body.p: I think that the revisions added in the re-revised version (see above) make this point clearer.

disp-quote.p: I applaud the authors on this large study and appreciate their thoughtful replies and the revised article.
